key_insight: Stagnation lines persist only when the local flow acceleration satisfies a compatibility condition; otherwise, they generally break into isolated stagnation points.
engineering_relevance: The framework can help track the motion and breakup of zero-velocity structures in simulated viscous, inviscid and compressible flows.
method: Differentiate the zero-velocity condition to relate line motion to local acceleration and the velocity gradient.
Invert the normal-plane gradient block to obtain normal motion, and test a scalar compatibility condition for persistence.
Specialize the theory to potential, Stokes, Navier–Stokes and compressible flows.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical results and exact examples, including acoustic-wave breakup and Navier–Stokes lines splitting into four points per period, rather than empirical validation.
watch_item: The normal-velocity formula requires an invertible normal-plane gradient block; degenerate points need separate analysis, and generic breakup is described only to first order in time.
paper_title: How stagnation lines move, persist and break up in fluid flows
